contributions.headingText: Pulmonary meningiomas are identical to meningothelial (arachnoidal) cell neoplasms that typically arise from dura mater of the CNS but are without a demonstrable CNS lesion.
2F71.3 & XH11P5 Neoplasms of uncertain behaviour of trachea, bronchus, or lung & Meningioma, NOS
There is no predilection for a specific anatomical site in the lung {8941002}.

Most cases are incidental, although some patients present with respiratory symptoms including haemoptysis {18486986}. Images shows slow-growing, well-circumscribed nodules on CT, with high metabolic activity on FDG PET {18486986}.
There is a slight female predominance. The median age is 56 years (range: 18–108 years) {19632430; 23443940; 30548187}.

Hypotheses include origin from pluripotent cells, heterotopic embryonic rests, and meningothelioid nodules {8941002; 18486986}. Although isolated meningothelioid nodules {15043310} lack mutation damage, multiple meningothelioid nodules show increased genetic alterations and may represent transition to neoplasia. Occasional meningiomas occur in the setting of multiple meningothelioid nodules {12365227}.
Most are solitary, well circumscribed, and firm, with a yellow-tan to grey cut surface. Size is markedly variable (median: 24 mm; range: 4–150 mm) {30548187; 9850654}.

Most tumours are well circumscribed and consist of a solid proliferation of tumour cells growing in whorls and lobular nests, most often with transitional or fibrous patterns. Rare examples of anaplastic {23443940; 24761155} and chordoid meningiomas are reported {15714337; 20634760; 30588452}. CNS criteria have been used for grading. Cells are positive for vimentin, EMA, PR, SSTR2A [[Louis DN, Ohgaki H, Wiestler OD, et al., editors. WHO classification of tumours of the central nervous system. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2016. (WHO classification of tumours series, 4th rev. ed.; vol. 1). https://publications.iarc.fr/543.]], and (rarely) S100 {30548187}. CD56 can be positive. Cytokeratin, other melanoma markers, and neuroendocrine markers are negative. Increased proliferation may be seen in anaplastic meningiomas {23443940}. Metastatic meningioma requires exclusion, as do spindle cell thymoma, solitary fibrous tumour, and monophasic synovial sarcoma, using appropriate immunohistochemistry {8941002}. Meningothelioid nodules are distinguished from meningiomas by their interstitial and frequently perivenular pattern of growth and ill-defined borders. In contrast to meningiomas, they typically lack a solid growth pattern and a sharply circumscribed border. Most meningothelioid nodules are ≤ 3 mm in size, but they can be as large as 5 mm {17414111; 2830799}.
Tumours can rarely be diagnosed by FNA {12365227}. The presence of intranuclear inclusions and psammoma bodies can create confusion with thyroid carcinoma {30548187}.

In the CNS, most meningiomas have allelic loss on chromosome 22 and NF2 mutations [[Louis DN, Ohgaki H, Wiestler OD, et al., editors. WHO classification of tumours of the central nervous system. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2016. (WHO classification of tumours series, 4th rev. ed.; vol. 1). https://publications.iarc.fr/543.]].

Essential:

  • A circumscribed solid proliferation of tumour cells growing in whorls and lobular nests, most often with transitional or fibrous patterns
  • Absence of CNS disease with histological and immunohistochemical features of CNS meningioma
  • Lack of predominant interstitial or perivenular distribution, ill-defined borders
  • Size usually > 4 mm
Most tumours show indolent growth. Rare aggressive behaviour is associated with atypical or anaplastic features (WHO grades II–III) {10366156; 23443940}.
